Discussion

Study 1 provides initial evidence that friendship bids are subject to self-other asymmetries: people expect others to judge their bids more negatively (and less positively when controlling for other negative dimensions) than they judge others' bids. Attribute ratings revealed a hierarchical, three-factor structure: one positive (e.g., friendly) and two negative dimensions: hesitant-negative (e.g., anxious) and assertive-negative (e.g., pushy). This structure suggests that pessimistic expectations about friendship bids may reflect distinct concerns about how these attempts may be interpreted from different perspectives. Study 1 has several limitations. First, the between-subjects design prevented estimating the stability of the asymmetry within individuals. Second, it remains unclear whether the null finding for positive ratings reflects true absence of asymmetry or whether it emerges only when individuals take both perspectives.

Third, Study 1 did not link perceptions to any downstream social decisions.

Study 2

Study 2 adopts a within-subjects design and extends Study 1 in two ways. First, it quantifies the stability of this self-other asymmetry as a construal. Second, it examines whether positive, hesitant-negative, and assertive-negative attribute perceptions predict two anticipated social behaviors: likelihood that the asker would extend the imagined invitation and likelihood of acceptance by the recipient.

Methods

Participants

Using the smallest effect size identified in Study 1 (𝑑=.28), we estimated 140 participants would be sufficient for a within-subjects design. A final sample of 154 undergraduates (detectable d = 0.45, dz = 0.23) participated for course credit through the psychology participant pool.

Procedure

Participants completed both asker and recipient conditions in randomized order, with three randomly selected vignettes per condition. Participants completed all three vignettes from one condition before switching. Vignettes were sampled without replacement, so no participant saw both versions of the same vignette. After each vignette, participants rated how the recipient would evaluate the asker using the reduced set of 11 attributes and reported willingness to initiate and anticipated acceptance. Finally, participants completed measures of Big Five personality, state attachment, social exploration-exploitation tendencies, and demographics.

Measures

Friendship Initiation Vignettes. We retained 16 of the 17 original vignettes from Study 1. One vignette elicited substantially higher ratings across hesitant-negative attributes, suggesting participants may have construed it very differently from the other vignettes (see supplementary materials). To preserve construct comparability, we excluded this vignette in subsequent studies.

We also underlined the key initiation behavior in each vignette (e.g., "One day, you ask them if they want to grab a coffee after class") for later reference (see Willingness to Initiate).

Social Role Manipulation.

The random assignment to asker or recipient condition remains the same as in Study 1, except all participants saw both conditions.

Evaluative Attributes.

To streamline measurement and minimize participant burden, we reduced the 24 attributes to 11 by balancing three criteria: EGA-based redundancy, EFA loadings, and theoretical relevance. First, EGA's unique variate function identifies locally dependent items, and with redundancy > .25 between two items suggests one can be removed while preserving the identified structure (Christensen et al., 2023). Second, we also prioritized items with primary loadings ≥ .50 and minimal cross-loadings. Third, we considered theoretical relevance to the interpersonal context. Final decisions balanced all three criteria (see Figure 2B).

For instance, although both uneasy and socially awkward showed EFA cross-loadings, socially awkward was retained because it contributed more uniquely to the EGA structure. While happy (.68) had slightly higher loading than friendly (.63), we retained friendly for greater interpersonal relevance.

Anticipated Social Behaviors.

Willingness to Initiate.

For each vignette, participants rated their own willingness to initiate (asker condition) or their perception of their partner's willingness to do so (recipient condition) on a 1-7 Likert scale. As asker, participants saw: "If this scenario happened to you in real life, how likely would you be to take the underlined initiative?" As recipient, participants saw: "If this scenario happened to you in real life, how likely would it be that the other person would take the underlined initiative?" Anticipated Acceptance. For each vignette, participants also rated the likelihood of their partner accepting the invitation (asker condition) or their own likelihood of accepting the invitation (recipient condition) on a 1-7 Likert scale. As asker, participants saw: "Assuming that you did take the underlined initiative, how likely do you think the other person would agree to the invite?" As recipient, participants saw: "Assuming that you did take the underlined initiative, how likely would you be to agree to the invite?"

Covariates. In addition to Big Five personality (α = .72-.81) and state attachment (α = .84-.90), we administered the Social Exploration-Exploitation Questionnaire (Tsang et al., under review), which captures individual differences in people's tendency to expand their social network (exploration) versus invest in existing ties (exploitation). Participants indicated agreement with 11 statements on a 1-7 Likert scale, such as "I seek out opportunities to meet new people" (exploration subscale, α = .84) and "I tend to just stick with the friends that I have" (exploitation subscale, α = .77). We calculated average scores for each subscale.

Data Analysis and Hypotheses

We first confirmed perception structure using confirmatory factor analysis. Our primary model used a hybrid bifactor structure. All seven loaded on a general negative factor, while hesitant and assertive dimensions were represented by two orthogonal subfactors uncorrelated with the general negative factor. Four positive items loaded on a separate positive facto, which was allowed to correlate with the general negative factor. This structure therefore distinguishes overall negative evaluation from qualitatively distinct negative concerns, rather than testing the two negative dimensions as entirely separate correlated factors. We compared this bifactor model against simpler one-, two-, and three-factor orthogonal and correlated alternatives. Parallel analysis, EGA, EFA, and PCA were reported as supplementary analyses.

Next, similar to Study 1, we conducted separate mixed-effects models predicting each dimension rating from condition, with random intercepts for participants and vignettes and random slopes of condition by participant and vignette. For each model, we calculated participant-and vignette-level ICCs.

We also examined whether perceptions predicted willingness to initiate and anticipated acceptance. For each dimension, we calculated each participant's mean perception score across all vignettes and both conditions (between-person predictor) and a deviation score for each rating from their mean (within-person predictor). These scores were entered simultaneously with condition and their interactions in two mixed-effects models to predict the vignette-level outcomes. Main effects indicate how each perception dimension relates to overall anticipated social behavior, holding others constant. Thus, these coefficients reflect its unique association with anticipated social behavior after accounting for overlap with the other dimensions. Rating × condition interactions indicate whether these relationship strengths differ by social role (asker or recipient). Finally, we tested robustness following Study 1 procedures.

We expected to replicate Study 1 findings that meta-perceptions are more negative and less positive than other-perceptions (H1) and that the hybrid bifactor structure would be the bestperforming model (H2). We expected variance in ratings would be predominantly attributable to stability within the same individuals rather than vignette variation (H3). We further hypothesized that perceptions of attributes would predict the magnitude of this asymmetry in willingness to initiate (H4.1) and anticipated acceptance (H4.2), though we had no a priori predictions about which attribute dimensions would matter most. All analyses were preregistered except H2.

SELF-OTHER ASYMMETRIES IN FRIENDSHIP BIDS

Although the analysis for H3 was preregistered, we did not specify a corresponding hypothesis.

(https://aspredicted.org/3sww-tdtd.pdf).

Results

Number of Evaluative Attribute Dimensions

The hybrid bifactor model demonstrated superior fit across all criteria, including CFI, TLI, RMSEA, and SRMR, with the lowest AIC and BIC (see supplementary materials for the complete model comparisons). Because only the three-factor correlated model is nested within the bifactor model, a chi-square difference test was conducted, further supporting the bifactor model (Δχ² = 45.51, Δdf = 7, p < .001). Exploratory analyses also supported a similar threefactor structure (full information in supplementary materials). The superiority of the bifactor model suggests that the relationships between the two negative dimensions are best captured through a hierarchical structure.

Effects of Social Role Manipulation on Meta-Perceptions

First, the within-subjects design allowed us to compute a self-other asymmetry score for each attribute dimension (see Figure 3). Consistent with Study 1, participants reported significantly higher ratings on both negative dimensions when in the asker condition than in the recipient condition (Table 3). Note. Each histogram shows the distribution of self-other asymmetry scores (asker -recipient ratings) for an attribute dimension across Studies 2-5. Percentages in red indicate the proportion of participants who showed a critical bias against themselves.

For the positive dimension, this reflects a positive bias towards the other. For the hesitant-negative and assertive-negative dimensions, this reflects a negative bias against the self. While the sample averages generally reflect a self-critical bias, the histograms illustrate the breadth of variation across individuals. Full distributions of asymmetry directions (self-favoring, other-favoring, and no asymmetry) are reported in the supplementary materials.

Different from Study 1, condition also significantly predicted positive ratings.

Participants rated others' bids more positively than their own. Because this effect was not significant in Study 1's between-subjects design, we wondered whether it emerges only when participants compare how positive an impression they make relative to others. Put differently, does the within-subjects design prompt participants to compare themselves to an imagined friendly, charming initiator, thereby leading them to judge themselves more harshly? If so, the order in which participants completed the asker and recipient conditions should matter.

To test this, we fitted an exploratory model (not preregistered) predicting positive ratings from condition (asker versus recipient), condition order (asker-first versus recipient-first), and their interaction. The interaction was significant, b = -0.35, SE = 0.08, t(153) = -4.43, p < .001, but not the main effect of condition, b = -0.08, SE = 0.06, t(148) = -1.50, p = .135. Simple slope analyses revealed that the self-other asymmetry emerged only when participants first imagined receiving an invitation (recipient condition) and then imagined extending one themselves (asker condition), b = -0.42, SE = 0.07, t(920) = -6.09, p < .001; no asymmetry emerged in the opposite order, b = 0.08, SE = 0.07, t(920) = 1.20, p = .232 (see supplementary materials for details). This pattern suggests that unlike negative attributions, which operate as an absolute asymmetry against the self, positive meta-perceptions may become self-devaluing primarily when participants can directly compare another person's initiation with their own. Similar to Study 1, most variance in attribute ratings (56.0%-65.1%) was attributable to participant differences compared to only 0.5%-2.5% to vignette differences. In contrast, less variance in willingness to initiate and anticipated acceptance was attributable to participant differences and more to vignette differences (Table 3). These findings confirm that self-other asymmetries in friendship bid perceptions reflect a generalized, schema-like expectation that carries across different scenarios and is very resistant to variation in the specific actions and contexts involved. Condition remained significant in all robustness checks.

Association Between Meta-Perceptions and Anticipated Social Behaviors

Willingness to Initiate. At the between-person level, participants who generally evaluated initiators more positively reported a greater perceived likelihood of initiation (see Table 4 5). This effect was stronger in the asker condition when people reported their own willingness to initiate. At the within-person level, higher-than-average positive meta-perceptions were marginally associated with higher anticipated likelihood of initiation, with the effect stronger as the asker. Moreover, higher-than-average assertive-negative perceptions were linked to lower perceived likelihood of initiation within-person, with the effect stronger as the asker.

Anticipated Acceptance.

At the between-person level, participants who generally evaluated initiators more positively were more optimistic about acceptance. At the within-person level, both higher-than-average positive and hesitant-negative ratings predicted greater anticipated acceptance, whereas higher-than-average assertive-negative ratings predicted the opposite. Only the effects of positive and assertive-negative ratings were stronger when participants were the asker.

Discussion

Study 2 replicated the hierarchical, three-dimensional structure of perceptions and demonstrated that positive self-other asymmetry emerges only through social comparison.

People believed that they would be perceived less positively than others in friendship bids only if they first imagined a hypothetical other's attempt. One possibility is that negative attributes may be more internalized or context-insensitive. Alternatively, the "imagined other" may serve as an idealized comparison target that makes the self seem less positive (friendly, confident) by contrast.

Overall, the self-other asymmetries across the three dimensions were highly stable within participants across scenarios and more stable than anticipated outcomes, such as anticipated acceptance of the friendship bid. This pattern suggests that friendship bid perceptions may reflect a relatively consistent construal tendency or relational schema.

These perceptions also predicted anticipated social behaviors at both between-and within-person levels. Overall, more positive perceptions were associated with more optimistic expectations (i.e., that initiation would occur, and invitations would be well received), whereas more assertive-negative perceptions were linked to the opposite. These effects were typically stronger when participants imagined themselves as askers. This suggests that people see their own bids as more contingent on other's evaluations. Notably, greater hesitant-negative metaperceptions predicted more favorable expectations that initiation would happen, which provides further evidence that the two negative dimensions function differentially. We discuss these findings in the General Discussion.

Although vignette-based studies offer strong control over the content of friendship bids, they require participants to evaluate imagined interactions with hypothetical partners. Study 3 therefore moves to a more naturalistic interpersonal context by examining perceptions of specific peers whom participants had repeatedly interacted with in a program designed to foster social connection.

Study 3

Study 3 was a field study conducted using a dyadic/group dataset from an evidence-based belonging intervention course at a public university in the Southeastern United States (Costello et al., 2022). Participants met weekly in small groups of 6-10 students led by trained facilitators and completed structured activities designed to build social-connection skills, increase belonging, and foster relationships with other students. By the time of the study, group members had met six times, providing both meaningful friendship potential and a relatively standardized amount of prior contact across peers. This setting therefore allowed us to examine friendship bid expectations about familiar, plausible friendship partners while holding prior exposure more constant than would typically be possible in naturally occurring relationships.

Study 3 serves three goals. First, it examines whether self-other asymmetries generalize beyond hypothetical scenarios to an ecologically valid context. Second, it tests whether the hierarchical, three-dimensional structure observed in the vignette studies also describes people's expectations for real interaction partners, rather than only their abstract beliefs about social norms. Third, it tests the predictive power of the three dimensions for specific targets with whom the participants have ongoing acquaintanceships.

Procedure and Participants

Approximately one month into the semester, the research team invited students enrolled in a one-credit belonging-focused course to participate in a psychology research study. About two weeks later, consenting students completed a group-specific survey, which was customized to include the first names of all consenting students in that group. Participants first identified which consenting classmates they already considered friends. For each nonfriend classmate, participants completed other-perception and meta-perception ratings in a potential friendshipinitiation scenario. Specifically, they first imagined that the classmate asked them to hang out outside of class, then imagined asking the classmate to hang out. In total, 59 participants consented and 51 completed the survey across 19 groups. The number of participating students per section ranged from 2 to 5, yielding 198 valid dyadic observations (detectable d = 0.73, dz = 0.37). Each participant received $10 for successful completion.

Measures

Evaluative Attribute. Same as Study 2.

Willingness to Initiate. Same as Study 2.

Anticipated Acceptance. Same as Study 2.

Data Analysis and Hypotheses

For analyses overlapping with Study 2, we used the same analytic approach and expected replication. Mixed-effects models included random intercepts for unique dyads and for participants nested within course sections when models converged. For analyses predicting willingness to initiate and anticipated acceptance, each observation represented a specific participant-partner pair. Unlike Study 2, however, we did not separate between-and withinperson associations because 20 of the 51 participants contributed only one nonfriend rating, leaving insufficient within-person variation. We therefore modeled the three evaluative dimensions directly as predictors of dyad-specific outcomes. This approach parallels the between-person analyses in Study 2 while accounting for the different data structure of Study 3.

Accordingly, these outcome analyses should be interpreted as supplementary participant-level tests. (All analyses were preregistered except the between-person outcome effects: https://aspredicted.org/sv4bk9.pdf)

Results

Number of Evaluative Attribute Dimensions

The bifactor model demonstrated superior fit across all criteria (see supplementary materials for model fit) and fitted better than three-factor (Δχ² = 17.20, Δdf = 7, p = .016).

Effects of Social Role Manipulation on Meta-Perceptions

Consistent with predictions, participants reported lower positive ratings as well as higher hesitant-and assertive-negative ratings as the asker than as the recipient (Table 3).

Association Between Meta-Perceptions and Anticipated Social Behaviors

Willingness to Initiate. Participants who generally evaluated initiators more positively reported greater perceived likelihood of initiation (b = 0.29, SE = 0.13, t(91) = 2.28, p =.025),

We did not observe any other significant main effect or interaction (see supplementary materials for full details).

Anticipated Acceptance.

Participants who generally evaluated initiators more positively were more optimistic about acceptance (b = 0.44, SE = 0.13, t(92) = 3.52, p <.001), while those who generally evaluated initiators as more assertive-negative were less optimistic (b = -0.78, SE = 0.18, t(88) = -4.26, p <.001). The effect for assertive-negative perceptions was stronger when people were the asker (b = 0.80, SE = 0.31, t(61) = 2.62, p = 0.011). We did not observe a significant main effect or interaction for hesitant-negative perceptions.

Discussion

Study 3 replicated the self-other asymmetry of friendship bid expectations in a relatively ecologically valid setting where people had repeated interactions and friendship could emerge. It also replicated the hierarchical, three-dimensional structure of perceptions, suggesting that these dimensions reflect meaningfully distinct facets of a relational schema even in real life. Consistent with Study 2, positive and assertive-negative perceptions predicted anticipated social behavior better than hesitant-negative perceptions. More positive perceptions were linked to greater willingness to initiate and greater anticipated acceptance, whereas more assertive-negative perceptions were linked to lower anticipated acceptance. The effect of assertive-negative perceptions was stronger when participants imagined themselves as the asker, suggesting that concerns about seeming pushy or needy may constrain one's own prosocial intentions more than they shape judgments of others. Hesitant-negative perceptions were not consistently associated with these outcomes. Together, these findings further support the distinctiveness of the three dimensions and their different implications for anticipated friendship bid behavior in a real-world setting with actual potential friends.

A limitation of Studies 2-3 is that outcome variables were based on anticipated behaviors in hypothetical scenarios. It remains unclear whether people's construal about friendship bids relates to real-world social outcomes, such as actual network size.

Study 4

Study 4 expanded prior studies by examining participants' real-world social networks (e.g., network size) and friendship behaviors. As a behavioral indicator of actual initiation tendencies, participants reported who initiated their most recent friendship (self or other). We also tested an educational and writing intervention designed to increase awareness of self-other asymmetries and to assess whether this would lead to a greater likelihood to sign up for an ostensible friendship app. The intervention failed to affect any outcomes. Qualitative coding indicated a manipulation failure: over half of participants did not fully understand the message of the educational intervention. Full details on the intervention, including descriptive statistics, coding procedures, and results, are available in the supplementary materials. Because the intervention occurred at the very end of the study, it did not affect any of the analyses reported here.

Methods

Participants

Because the expected effect size of a self-other asymmetry in friendship bid expectations on interpersonal outcomes was unknown, we recruited as many participants as possible within university participant pool limits. In total, 267 participants were recruited. Study 4 was conducted in two phases. Initially, we collected data from 214 participants (Study 4a) to confirm the bifactor structure identified in Studies 1-2 using a reduced 8-item scale. However, factor analyses revealed suboptimal model fit, likely due to insufficient items per specific factor (see Results). We therefore reverted to the 11-item scale and collected an additional 53 participants (Study 4b) primarily to confirm the bifactor structurefoot_1 . Given that both subsamples used identical procedures, we pooled participants (N = 267, detectable d = 0.34, dz = 0.17) for all analyses to maximize statistical power, with study phase included as a covariate in all analyses. We calculated average attribute ratings using the shared 8-item scale for all participants to maintain measurement consistency. This approach is consistent with recommended practice in multi-phase designs (Hofer & Piccinin, 2009). Study phase was not a significant predictor in any model.

Procedure

Participants completed a procedure similar to Study 2. They also described how they and their most recent friend met and completed the social network measures. Participants were then randomly assigned to either control or writing educational intervention condition, and all were introduced to an ostensible friendship app.

Measures

Friendship Initiation Vignettes. Same as Study 2.

Social Role Manipulation. Same as Studies 1 and 2.

Evaluative Attributes.

Based on the item reduction results from Study 2, the final set included 8 attributes. We used the same three criteria as Study 2 in deciding which item to keep.

We removed warm, reserved, and desperate for Study 4a.

Willingness to Initiate. Same as Study 2.

Anticipated Acceptance. Same as Study 2.

Proactiveness in Most Recent Friendship. Participants described how they and their most recent friend met in an open-ended response (minimum 100 characters). Responses were coded on a three-level scale reflecting participants' proactiveness in real-world friendship initiation: -1 = friend was more proactive (e.g., the friend introduced themselves, started the conversation, or asked to hang out; 18.4% of responses),0 = both parties showed similar initiative (50.3%), and1 = participant was more proactive (31.2%). Five undergraduate research assistants served as coders. Each response was independently coded by two randomly paired assistants. To establish reliability and refine the codebook, all five assistants first coded a random subset of 50 responses, achieving excellent interrater reliability (Cohen's κ = .81). The assistants then independently coded the remaining responses using the finalized codebook. The first author resolved all discrepancies, and these reconciled codes were used in the analyses. Full coding procedures and sample responses are in the supplementary materials.

Social Network Measures.

Participants listed their friends' first names, with 12 initial slots provided. They could report up to 100 friends by manually adding slots. For each friend, participants reported gender, race/ethnicity, closeness (0-100 slider), who typically initiates hangouts ("I do," "My friend does," or "Roughly 50/50"), and whether the friend was also friends with other named friends. These measures allowed us to calculate the following metrics (descriptive data in supplementary materials):  Network size: The number of friends listed.

 Average closeness: Sum of closeness scores divided by number of friends.

 Network density: Proportion of ties between friends divided by total possible ties (0 indicates none of the participant's friends are friends with each other; 1 indicates all friends are friends with each other).

 Racial homophily: Percentage of friends belonging to the same racial/ethnic group as the participant.

 Average proactiveness in existing friendships: Proportion of friendships in which the participant self-reports initiating most hangouts.

Covariates. same as Study 1 (Big Five personality, α = .72-.81; state attachment, α =.86-.90).

Data Analysis and Hypotheses

For analyses overlapping with Study 2, we followed the same analytical approach and expected replication 5 . For each new outcome, participants' average ratings on the three perception dimensions within each condition (asker and recipient) served as a total of six predictors. Linear regressions were used for continuous outcomes (network size and average closeness). Beta regressions were used for proportion-based outcomes bounded between 0 and 1 (network density, racial homophily, and average proactiveness in friendships). Ordinal regression was used for proactiveness in most recent friendship formation. We hypothesized that individuals' perceptions of friendship initiation would meaningfully predict these interpersonal outcomes (H5.3-H5.5), though we did not preregister which attribute dimension would show the strongest effects. (See the full preregistration here: https://aspredicted.org/uc5h42.pdf . )

Results

Number of Evaluative Attribute Dimensions

In Study 4a with 8 items, the hybrid bifactor model performed similarly to the threefactor correlated models (Δχ² = 4.22, Δdf = 5, p =.518), though the bifactor model had great model fit indices and yielded the lower AIC and BIC than all other models (see supplementary materials). It is possible that a smaller pool of items may have rendered estimation of the bifactor model unstable. As such, in Study 4b, we re-adopted the 11-item scale from Study 2. Consistent with expectations, the bifactor model demonstrated superior fit across all criteria and outperformed the three-factor correlated model (Δχ² = 27.31, Δdf = 7, p < .001). Exploratory analyses also supported a similar structure (see the supplementary materials).

Effects of Social Role Manipulation on Meta-Perceptions

Consistent with predictions, participants reported lower positive ratings as well as higher hesitant-and assertive-negative ratings as the asker than as the recipient. (Condition remained significant in all robustness checks.) Similar to Study 2, most variance in attribution dimensions was attributable to stable participant differences (60.3%-65.1%), with little variance attributable to vignette differences (0.8%-2.2%). In contrast, anticipated social behaviors showed lower participant-level variance (see Table 3). This pattern suggests that the self-other asymmetries in friendship bid expectations operate largely as stable construal tendencies.

Association Between Meta-Perceptions and Anticipated Social Behaviors

Willingness to Initiate. Similar to Study 2, at the between-person level, participants who generally evaluated initiators more positively reported greater perceived likelihood of initiation, with this effect stronger in the asker condition (see Table 4 5). At the within-person level, higher-than-average positive ratings predicted greater anticipation of initiation, while higherthan-average assertive-negative ratings predicted the opposite. However, these effects were no longer stronger in the asker condition.

Anticipated Acceptance. Consistent with Study 2, at the between-person level, participants who generally evaluated initiators more positively were more optimistic about acceptance. Study 4 also revealed that participants who generally evaluated initiators as more assertive-negative were less optimistic. At the within-person level, higher-than-average positive ratings predicted greater anticipated acceptance, whereas higher-than-average assertive-negative ratings predicted the opposite. Contrary to Study 2, hesitant-negative perceptions did not predict anticipated acceptance, and no effects were stronger in the asker condition.

Association Between Meta-Perceptions and Real-World Friendships

Proactiveness in Most Recent Friendship. Participants' average assertive-negative ratings as the recipient positively predicted self-reported proactiveness in forming their most recent friendship (b = 0.73, SE = 0.30, z = 2.47, p = .014). The more participants perceived those who initiated with them as pushy, needy, or creepy, the more likely they were to report being the proactive one in their own friendship formation (see Figure 4).

Figure 4

Other-Perceptions of Negative Attributes Predict Proactiveness in Recent Friendship Note. Only significant predictors are visualized. Studies 4 and 5 measured proactiveness using different scales and therefore have different y-axis ranges. In Study 4, proactiveness reflects the predicted probability (ranging from 0 to 1) that a response falls into the "more proactive" category as a function of each predictor. In Study 5, proactiveness reflects participants' average ratings across three slider items (ranging from 1 to 100) assessing self-reported initiation tendencies. Across both studies, greater negative other-perceptions predicted greater selfreported proactiveness in forming participants' most recent friendship. For a complete visualization of all three proactiveness categories in Study 4, see the supplementary materials.

Social Network Measures.

Among social network metrics, only network size showed significant association with perceptions of friendship bids. Specifically, hesitant-negative metaperceptions predicted opposite associations with network size depending on social role.

Participants' average hesitant-negative ratings as the asker predicted larger network size (b = 1.00, SE = 0.43, t(259) = 2.34, p = 0.020), whereas the same ratings in the recipient condition predicted smaller networks (b = -1.74, SE = 0.66, t(259) = -2.65, p = .009). People who believe others see them as awkward, anxious, and reserved during friendship invitations have larger networks (controlling for other dimensions), while people who see others this way have smaller networks (see Figure 5). For null results on other network metrics, see supplementary materials.

Figure 5

Predictors of Network Size Note. Associations between friendship bid perceptions and self-reported network size differed across samples. In the undergraduate sample, greater hesitant-negative meta-perceptions predicted larger networks, whereas greater hesitant-negative other-perceptions predicted smaller networks. In the community sample, only more positive meta-perceptions predicted larger networks; other-perceptions were not associated with network size.

Discussion

Study 4 replicated the structure of the self-other asymmetry in friendship bid expectations as a stable construal tendency across contexts. Overall, positive and assertive-negative attribute perceptions consistently predicted anticipated initiation and acceptance behaviors. However, compared to Study 2, these associations were not always stronger in the asker condition, and effects for hesitant-negative perceptions were less stable across outcomes. Thus, although participants were self-critical, their negative evaluations of imagined others predicted anticipated social behaviors to a similar extent as their meta-evaluations of themselves.

Study 4 linked evaluations in imagined scenarios to two real-world social outcomes: proactiveness in most recent friendship and social network size. First, participants who perceived others initiating with them as more pushy, needy, or creepy described themselves as more proactive in forming their own most recent friendship. Second, believing one's own initiation might come across as awkward or anxious was associated with reporting more friends, whereas perceiving others' initiation with those attributes was linked to having fewer friends. While we offer theoretical interpretations in the General Discussion, the findings provide clear evidence that other-perceptions and meta-perceptions of friendship bids differentially predict meaningful real-life outcomes. Yet, because Studies 1-3 relied exclusively on undergraduate samples, a critical open question is whether these relationships generalize to broader adult populations.

Study 5

Study 5 recruited an older, more nationally representative U.S. sample to test the generalizability of the findings beyond college-aged participants. Age may meaningfully shape friendship bid perceptions because older adults have greater accumulated experience navigating relationships and may be less sensitive to social evaluation, potentially reducing self-other asymmetries (Fields et al., 2021; Hoffman et al., 2021). We therefore tested whether age moderated this asymmetry and whether associations between friendship initiation perceptions and the two significant interpersonal outcomes identified in Study 4-network size and selfreported proactiveness in most recent friendship-replicate in this broader sample.

Methods

Participants

Power analyses were based on significant between-person effects observed in Study 4 for network size (f² = .031). To detect this effect with 80% power at α = .05, 254 participants were required.

Because the ordinal regression model predicting proactiveness in Study 4 would require a larger sample to detect comparable effects, we adapted the measure to a continuous format (linear regression) to balance feasibility and statistical power. In total, we recruited 261 adults (M age = 46.21, SD age = 13.8, min = 19, max = 78, detectable d = 0.35, dz = 0.17) through Prolific for $1.80 in compensation. All participants were native English speakers born and currently residing in the United States, representing 42 states (see supplementary materials for full distribution). Procedures Participants followed a procedure similar to Study 4. After completing vignette-based tasks, they completed network and proactiveness measures, followed by the Big Five inventory and demographic questions. Measures Friendship Initiation Vignette. To develop study materials suitable for an older sample, we used a large language model (OpenAI's GPT-5) to generate new vignettes. We created three versions of the generation prompt differing in example detail: no examples, brief generic setting examples, and with undergraduate vignettes. Each version was run iteratively to maximize output diversity. All vignettes were compiled and reviewed by the research team, who selected those best reflecting realistic and relatable friendship initiation contexts for adult participants. Full prompt wording and selected vignettes are in supplementary materials. Below are two examples: Example 1: "At your neighborhood dog park, you notice someone with a dog that often plays with yours. One day, you two start chatting about your pets." Example 2: "You and another member of your religious community always see each other at the same community events. At one of the gatherings, you two exchange some comments and have a good conversation." Social Role Manipulation. Same as Studies 1-3. Evaluative Attribute. Same as Studies 2 and 3b. Willingness to Initiate. Same as Study 2-3. Anticipated Acceptance. Same as Study 2-3.

Proactiveness in Most Recent Friendship. Participants described how they met their most recent friend (as in Study 4) and rated their proactiveness using three items on a 0-100 slider scale, with higher scores reflecting greater initiative (example item: "Thinking about the friend you just described, who took the lead in getting the friendship started?"). Internal consistency was high (α = .81). See supplementary materials for full item wording.

Network Size.

Same as Study 4 (M = 5.59, SD = 3.34, min = 0, max = 12).

Covariate. Due to time constraints, only a shortened version of the Big Five Personality Scale (Rammstedt & John, 2007, α = .54-.85) was administered.

Data Analysis and Hypotheses

Study 5 followed the same data analysis approach as Study 4, with three modifications.

First, to examine age effects, we tested interactions between age and condition when predicting participants' positive, hesitant-negative, assertive-negative ratings, willingness to initiate, and anticipated acceptance. We hypothesized age would moderate differences in these ratings (H4).

Second, we conducted an additional robustness check controlling for how self-relevant participants judged each vignette (e.g., people without dogs might not relate to a dog park vignette). Third, we used linear regression rather than ordinal regression to analyze self-reported Note. The bottom-right panel shows the age distribution (histogram) for the Study 5 sample.

Older participants reported more positive and less negative perceptions, as well as more optimistic anticipated social behavior, particularly as the asker. This reduced the discrepancy between meta-perceptions and other-perceptions, indicating a smaller self-critical bias.

Association Between Meta-perceptions and Anticipated Social Behaviors

Willingness to Initiate. All six main effects were significant (see Table 4 -5). At the between-person level, participants who generally evaluated initiators more positively expected initiation to be more likely to occur, consistent with Studies 2-3. While evaluating initiators generally as more hesitant-negative was also associated with greater expectation for initiation to occur, assertive-negative ratings were linked to the opposite. The effects of hesitant-negative and assertive-negative ratings were stronger as the asker. At the within-person level, when participants viewed the initiator as more assertive-negative than usual, they expected initiation to be less likely, consistent with Studies 2-3. When participants saw the initiator more positively than usual, they expected initiation to be more likely. Higher-than-average hesitant-negative ratings were also associated with reduced likelihood of initiation (nonsignificant in college samples). Unlike Studies 2-3, there was no significant interaction between positive ratings and condition. Instead, the effects of assertive-negative ratings were stronger as the asker at both between-and within-person levels.

Anticipated Acceptance.

Consistent with Studies 2-3, at the between-person level, participants who generally evaluated initiators more positively were more optimistic that initiation would be accepted. Consistent with Study 4, participants who generally evaluated initiators as more assertive-negative were less optimistic. Surprisingly, hesitant-negative ratings also significantly predicted greater anticipated acceptance. At the within-person level, higherthan-average positive ratings predicted greater anticipated acceptance, whereas higher-thanaverage assertive-negative ratings predicted the opposite, consistent with Studies 2-3. Similar to Study 4, Study 5 observed no significant interactions.

Association Between Meta-Perceptions and Real-World Friendships

Proactiveness in Most Recent Friendship: Participants' average hesitant-negative ratings in the recipient condition (rather than assertive-negative, as observed in Study 4) positively predicted self-reported proactiveness in forming their most recent friendship (b = 6.25, SE = 2.81, t(243) = 2.22, p = .027). The more participants perceived those who initiated with them as reserved, anxious, or socially awkward, the more likely they were to report being the proactive one in their own friendship formation (see Figure 4).

Social Network Size:

Participants' average positive ratings as the asker (rather than hesitant-negative, as observed in Study 4) predicted larger network size (b = 1.10, SE = 0.43, t(252) = 2.58, p = 0.011). Believing one's own initiation may come across as confident, sociable, warm, and friendly was associated with reporting more friends (see Figure 5).

Discussion

Study 5 replicated important findings from Study 4 in an older, Prolific sample and identified a notable age effect. Older adults demonstrate smaller differences between how they believe others would judge their own friendship bids and how they themselves would judge others' bids. They also view their own and others' willingness to initiate friendships as more comparable, suggesting reduced asymmetries in expected social behavior. While age did not moderate the asker-recipient gap in judgments of anticipated acceptance, older people did report more optimistic expectations of their own invitation. We discuss implications in the General Discussion.

Across Studies 2-4, positive perceptions consistently predicted more optimal anticipated social behaviors at both between-and within-person levels, while assertive-negative ratings at the between-person level consistently predicted the opposite. These associations were not consistently stronger when participants imagined themselves as the asker. In Study 5, hesitantnegative perceptions emerged as a significant between-person predictor of more optimistic anticipation of both initiation and acceptance. Further, Prolific adults who viewed others initiating with them as more hesitant-negative described themselves as more proactive in forming their most recent friendship. A similar pattern, but with assertive-negative, was observed in college samples. Meanwhile, Prolific adults who perceived their own initiation as more positive reported larger social networks, whereas among younger adults in Study 4, it was hesitant-negative ratings as askers that predicted larger networks. We return to these discrepancies in the General Discussion.

General Discussion

Across five studies, participants consistently had asymmetrical expectations for both hypothetical and real social partners. Specifically, they expected others to judge their own friendship bids less favorably than they judged others' bids. This self-other asymmetry showed significant stability within-person across contexts while varying substantially between-person and declining among older people. We also consistently showed that this asymmetry is more complex than a single tendency to expect negative evaluation. Instead, perceptions around friendship bids show a hierarchical, three-dimensional structure: positive, hesitant-negative, and assertive-negative. These dimensions differentially predicted both anticipated social decisions and longer-term friendship outcomes. Together, these findings position a self-other asymmetry in friendship bid expectations as a multidimensional, stable construal of social approach with consequences for whether, and how, people connect.

Generalized Relational Construal of Friendship Bids

Consistent with established research on self-critical biases (Boothby et al., 2018; Cooney et al., 2022; Reece et al., 2023; Welker et al., 2023), people expected others to judge them more negatively or less positively than they judge others for making similar friendship bids. On average, slightly more than half (57.9%) of participants showed a self-other asymmetry in friendship bids expectations, a proportion aligning with prior work (Elsaadawy & Carlson, 2022; Sprecher, 2025; Tissera et al., 2025), although its prevalence varied substantially across dimensions and samples (37% to 73%). The present findings extend this literature by showing that these asymmetries emerge before an interaction occurs, when no feedback from a partner is yet available.

Across varied scenarios-inviting a classmate for coffee, asking a neighbor on a dog walk, or suggesting lunch with a colleague-people showed substantial consistency in how they anticipated their own bids would be evaluated and how they would evaluate the bids of others.

This pattern indicates that these perceptions are not merely reflecting the appropriateness of particular social acts or context-specific reactions. Rather, people seem to bring a generalized, self-referential construal to new friendship opportunities and apply it across contexts. We conceptualize this tendency as a relatively proximal form of relational schema (Baldwin, 1992): a mental model of how the self operates within interpersonal relationships that guides expectations across friendship bid situations.

Notably, age emerged as a moderator of the self-other asymmetry in friendship bid expectations. Compared to younger adults, older adults show greater alignment between how they think others see their bids and how they evaluate others' bids, and this was consistent across both positive and negative attributes. They also reported being likelier to extend a friendship invitation and more optimistic that their invite would be well-received. These age effects may partly reflect older adults' greater experience successfully initiating (and receiving) friendship bids (Wrzus et al., 2013). It may also reflect age-related shifts in social motivation and emotional regulation. Socioemotional selectivity theory suggests older adults show greater emotional stability, more positive information processing (Luong et al., 2011), greater selectivity in interaction partners (Rolison & Lamarche, 2023), and less concern about negative evaluations (Fields et al., 2021; Hoffman et al., 2021). The age effect could also reflect generational changes in the normative acceptability of making friendship bids in person-younger adults are likelier to 2016). As we discuss below, assertive-negative meta-perceptions more consistently predicted social connection outcomes than hesitant-negative meta-perceptions. This suggests many missed friendship opportunities may be the product of a specific social threat: the fear of making others uncomfortable through one's attempt to connect.

Interpersonal Outcomes of Friendship Bid Perceptions

Across studies 2-5, the three dimensions of meta-and other-perceptions predicted anticipated social behaviors (i.e., likelihood of bid initiation and acceptance). People who viewed initiators more positively (friendly, warm, sociable, confident), both generally and relative to their typical perceptions, tended to judge bids as more likely to occur and be well received. In contrast, heightened assertive-negative perceptions (e.g., creepy) relative to one's typical perceptions were associated with lower willingness to initiate and more pessimistic expectations about acceptance. These findings suggest that momentary expectations about friendship bids could be shaped by how positively or negatively the act of reaching out is construed (Brudner et al., 2023). These associations were sometimes stronger when participants imagined themselves as the asker. Although this pattern was not consistent across studies, it raises the possibility that people view evaluations as more consequential for their own friendship bids than for others'. If so, they may underestimate how much similar evaluative concerns shape others' decisions to reach out.

Hesitant-negative perceptions showed a different pattern. Although they less consistently predicted anticipated social outcomes, when they did, higher hesitant-negative ratings predicted more positive social outcomes, at least when controlling for positive and assertive-negative ratings. This suggests that attributes like reserved, anxious, or socially awkward may carry relatively neutral-and sometimes even positive-interpersonal implications despite their negative valence. This divergence further reinforces the need to differentiate between these two forms of negative evaluation in friendship bids. We speculate that, once shared variance across the three attribute dimensions is controlled, anxiety or awkwardness can signal sincerity, investment, or affiliative concern and be well-received (Clegg, 2012; Feinberg et al., 2012). If this pattern replicates, it may point to a cognitive reframing opportunity for mild social anxiety: if others detect your anxiety or awkwardness when making a friendship bid, they may like you more.

Friendship bid perceptions were also linked to real-world friendship formation.

Unexpectedly, people who viewed others' friendship bids more negatively reported being more proactive in forming their most recent friendship. People who construe others' outreach more negatively may be less receptive to others' bids (Chen et al., 2012), leaving them with friendships that more often depend on their own initiation. Further complicating this unexpected finding, the specific negative dimension that predicted proactiveness in real-world friendships differed across samples. College students reported playing a more proactive role in their recent friendships if they perceived others' friendship bids as assertive-negative, while older Prolific samples reported so if they perceived others' friendship bids as hesitant-negative. Whether this is a cohort effect, an age effect, or a context effect-college is an unusual social environment-is a question for future work.

The attribute dimensions predicting network size also differed across samples. In the younger college sample, viewing oneself as reserved, anxious, and socially awkward was associated with larger social networks, while viewing others the same way predicted smaller networks. In contrast, in the older Prolific sample, only viewing oneself positively predicted larger networks. This divergence may reflect developmental shifts in social cognitive processes and motivational priorities. Compared to older adults, younger adults show greater attention to negative social information, potentially because they are still building their social identities and remain more sensitive to social standing (Benson & Elder, 2011; Gretarsdottir et al., 2004; Hoffman et al., 2021). For younger individuals, believing they come off as anxious or awkward may paradoxically signal greater social attunement and investment in social maintenance (Deng et al., 2024; Feinberg et al., 2012; Fisher et al., 2021). In contrast, seeing others this way may reflect heightened vigilance toward ambiguous cues (Chen et al., 2012). This likely leads to reduced receptivity to others' outreach and thus missed opportunities for connection. Conversely, older adults prioritize positive information and emotionally rewarding relationships (Fields et al., 2021; Isaacowitz et al., 2021; Thompson González et al., 2023). For them, positive metaperceptions may be especially important for sustaining social engagement.

Limitations and Future Directions

The present research has several limitations. First, our samples were predominantly White, U.S.-based, and most of the undergraduate participants came from relatively affluent backgrounds. Cultural norms surrounding friendship initiation (e.g., individualistic vs.

collectivistic expectations) may shape both meta-perceptions and their consequences. Members of marginalized groups may have lived experiences of identity-based social rejection (Hebl et al., 2012) that inform the risks they anticipate during such encounters. Second, the associations between perceptions and short-term social decisions did not consistently replicate across studies, particularly for hesitant-negative ratings. Future work should clarify when and for whom these associations are most robust.

Moreover, we did not directly test the causes of the observed self-other asymmetries. The observed age effect points to possibilities such as differences in attentional focus, accumulated social experience, and sensitivity to social evaluation. Future work should test these mechanisms more directly. Finally, although Study 3 moved beyond hypothetical targets by examining judgments of real peers with whom participants had repeated, meaningful interactions, the friendship bids themselves remained hypothetical, and the sample size was modest. Future research should examine actual friendship bids by measuring perceptions right before participants initiate with a specific peer with a bigger sample.

Conclusion

Across five studies, people expected that their own friendship bids would be perceived more negatively or less positively than comparable bids made by others. These self-other asymmetries emerged before interaction, generalized across varied friendship contexts, and reflected distinct types of negative concern with different interpersonal consequences. These findings illuminate a critical socio-cognitive barrier that may prevent acquaintances from beginning the delicate transition to friends.

Number of Evaluative Attribute Dimensions

The bifactor model outperformed the three-factor correlated model (Δχ² = 145.31, Δdf = 7, p < .001) and showed the best fit across all alternatives. This confirms that the distinction between positive, hesitant-negative, and assertive-negative dimensions is meaningful in older samples and that the relationship between the two negative dimensions is best captured through a hierarchical structure.

Effects of Social Role Manipulation and Age on Meta-Perceptions

Participants reported significantly lower positive, higher hesitant-negative, and higher assertive-negative ratings as the asker than as the recipient. The effect of condition remained significant in all robustness checks, including when controlling for applicability of vignettes (see supplementary materials). Most variance was attributable to participant rather than vignette differences. Notably, age significantly moderated the effect of condition for positive and hesitant-negative ratings (b = 0.01, SE = 0.002, t(247) = 2.65, p =0.009 and b = -0.01, SE = 0.003, t(247) = -2.39, p = 0.018, respectively), but only marginally significant for assertivenegative ratings (b = -0.005, SE = 0.003, t(247) = -1.90, p = 0.059) (see Figure 6). This means that older people may view their own and others' friendship bids more similarly. socialize and meet people online, but all our vignettes involved face-to-face bids (although it is not clear if online friendship bids have displaced in-person bids; McClain et al., 2026). Future work should explore whether age differences are due to developmental and experiential changes or a cohort effect, such as changing norms.

A Hierarchical Three-Dimensional Structure of Friendship Bid Perceptions

The hierarchical, three-dimensional structure of friendship bid perceptions challenges the assumption in prior liking gap work that perceptions around affiliative acts reflect one broad judgment of valence (e.g., Boothby et al., 2018; Cooney et al., 2022; Li et al., 2020). Moreover, these three dimensions do not map neatly onto an existing social cognition framework such as warmth and competence (Epley et al., 2022; Fiske et al., 2007).

One way to understand this structure is to begin with a two-dimensional model of valence, in which positive and negative evaluations are partially independent rather than opposite ends of a single continuum. A friendship bid can therefore be seen as potentially rewarding and/or potentially threatening. Our findings further suggest that, in an interaction, negative evaluations differentiate according to how the threat arises: the threat could be to the self or to the partner, and meta-perceptions reflect both. Hesitant-negative meta-perceptions (reserved, anxious, socially awkward) reflect a concern that the self seems threatened by the interaction, which is a well-studied concern in social anxiety (e.g., Ginat-Frolich et al., 2024). In contrast, assertive-negative concerns (needy, desperate, pushy, creepy), which are far less-studied, reflect a concern that the self is threatening to others. A "needy," "desperate," or "pushy" person may appear to pursue connection too demandingly (e.g., Gable, 2006) or in ways that infringe on a partner's autonomy. Judgments of "creepiness" in particular may arise when a person behaves unpredictably, making their intentions and potential for threat uncertain (McAndrew & Koehnke,

The raw Study 3 data include participant names and directed peer nominations within small course groups, which could enable identification when combined with group membership and demographic information. To protect participant confidentiality, we publicly shared only the cleaned, aggregated data.

Studies 4a and 4b were conducted during the same semester using the same participant pool, with no overlap in participants. We decided to collect additional participants because, near the end of the semester, the pool increased the number of recruitment credits available to each researcher.
